headline: Record profit of 1.3 billion, but the shares have halved
text: Schlumberger earned a record of about 1.35 billion dollars in 1982 on sales of 6.3 billion, a profit margin of 21 percent; no company among the world's 1,000 largest earned more. Yet its shares trade at about half their 1980 record, while the oil price is falling.
imageCaption: Entrance to Schlumberger's complex at Sugar Land, Texas

headline: Apple unveils the Lisa
text: Apple introduced the Lisa computer on 19 January. It is controlled with a mouse and pictures on the screen instead of typed commands and costs 9,995 dollars with a hard disk. Apple spent heavily to develop it and is betting it will win over business users.
imageCaption: "Evolution. Revolution.": Apple's advertisement for the Lisa, with the Apple II and Apple III above it, early 1983
imageCredit: Apple Computer advertisement, from Practical Computing, March 1983 (scan: nosher.net)

headline: Reagan's 'evil empire' and a shield in space
text: On 8 March President Reagan told a meeting of evangelical Christians in Orlando that the Soviet Union is 'the focus of evil in the modern world'. On 23 March, in a televised address, he called on American scientists to give the country the means of rendering nuclear missiles 'impotent and obsolete' with a defence, partly based in space, that could destroy them in flight. Senator Edward Kennedy mocked it as 'reckless Star Wars schemes', and the name Star Wars has stuck.
imageCredit: President (1981-1989 : Reagan). White House Photographic Office. 1981-1989

headline: Gold slumps after OPEC cuts the oil price
text: Gold averaged 420 dollars in March, 14 percent below February's 491. On 14 March OPEC cut its base oil price from 34 to 29 dollars a barrel, the first cut in its history, after twelve days of talks. US inflation is down to 3.5 percent (February), and the rate banks charge each other is still near 8.75 percent.
imageCaption: The UAE's oil minister Mana Saeed al-Otaiba with reporters at the OPEC meeting in London that cut the oil price, 7 March 1983
imageCredit: Photo by Jean Guichard/Sygma/Sygma via Getty Images

headline: The compact disc arrives in Europe
text: In March the compact disc and its players went on sale in Europe and America. Sony launched the format in Japan in October 1982 with its CDP-101 player at 168,000 yen; its partner Philips now brings its own player to Europe. A CD holds music as digital data read by a laser, without the hiss and scratches of tape and vinyl. Players and discs are still expensive.
imageCaption: The Sony CDP-101, one of the first compact disc players (1982-83)
imageCredit: Museo Nazionale della Scienza e della Tecnologia, Milan (see Commons file page)

headline: Berkshire's net worth rose 40% in 1982
text: Buffett's letter of 3 March reports that Berkshire's net worth rose 208 million dollars, or 40%, in 1982, to 737.43 dollars per share, a compound 22% a year over 18 years. He warns the percentage will diminish as Berkshire grows. The stock market has been rising since last August.
imageCaption: A See’s Candies shop, one of the businesses Berkshire Hathaway owns

headline: Tokyo Disneyland and the Disney Channel open
text: Tokyo Disneyland, the first Disney park outside the United States, opened on 15 April. It opens in a country on the rise: the Nikkei index of Japanese shares ended April at 8,637, 17% higher than a year ago. On 23 April Disney launched the Disney Channel on American cable television.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Walt_Disney_Company (read 2026-10-03); Nikkei 225 month-end levels: FRED series NIKKEI225, https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/NIKKEI225 (read 2026-10-04)

headline: Technology shares at a record
text: The Nasdaq index closed at a record 328.91 on 24 June, about 40% higher than at the start of the year. Computer and chip companies lead the rise: Intel gained about 30% in June alone. IBM has sold its PC far faster than it planned. The business behind the shares is growing fast: last year more than a hundred companies sold 2.8 million personal computers for 4.9 billion dollars. Apple's sales rose 74 percent to 583 million dollars, and Intel's reached a record 900 million.

headline: Siemens installs its first commercial MRI scanner
text: In August a Siemens MAGNETOM, the company's first commercial magnetic resonance scanner, went into operation at the Mallinckrodt Institute of Radiology in St. Louis after just under three months of installation. Siemens had tested a prototype at Hannover Medical School since February.

headline: Apple shares lose more than a third in a month
text: Apple's shares, which stood at 63 dollars in June, have collapsed: in September alone they lost 38%. Computer shares fell across the board after Osborne, a maker of portable computers, went bankrupt. Apple has troubles of its own: its new Lisa costs 10,000 dollars and sells poorly, it has cut the price of its best seller, the Apple IIe, and IBM, only two years after launching its PC, now sells more personal computers by value than Apple.

headline: The first mobile phone network opens in Chicago
text: The first call on a commercial cellular network was made in Chicago on 13 October, after the US regulator approved Motorola's handheld DynaTAC phone in September. Until now mobile phones have mostly been heavy sets built into cars; in Switzerland the PTT's portable Natel B phone weighs 12 kilograms and comes in a case.

headline: A BMW engine wins the Formula One title
text: Nelson Piquet won the Formula One drivers' championship on 15 October in South Africa, two points ahead of Alain Prost. His Brabham ran on a BMW turbocharged engine; it is the first title won with a turbo.
imageCaption: Nelson Piquet (Brabham-BMW, right) at the Dutch Grand Prix, Zandvoort, 28 August 1983

headline: The new American missiles arrive in Europe
text: The first US cruise missiles arrived at RAF Greenham Common in England on 13 November, and the first Pershing II launchers reached West Germany later in the month. The missiles are there so that NATO could hit the Soviet Union from western Europe in a war, just as the Soviet SS-20 missiles can hit western Europe. NATO decided in 1979 to station the missiles unless the Soviet Union scrapped its SS-20s; after the first Pershings arrived, the Soviet Union broke off the Geneva talks on medium-range weapons. Peace protesters have camped outside Greenham Common since 1981, and in April some 70,000 people formed a human chain there.
imageCaption: A Pershing II missile on a test launch, 1983

headline: America approves Sandimmune
text: The US Food and Drug Administration approved cyclosporin for clinical use on 14 November; Sandoz sells it as Sandimmune (Sandimmun in Switzerland). It damps the immune system so that the body does not reject a transplanted organ.
imageCaption: Structure of cyclosporin, the active substance of Sandoz's Sandimmune

headline: 'Nuclear winter': a nuclear war would darken and freeze the Earth
text: A group of scientists that includes the astronomer Carl Sagan published a study in the journal Science in late December: after a nuclear war, smoke and soot from burning cities would stay in the sky for years, block the sunlight and cool the whole planet. They call it 'nuclear winter'. Harvests would fail everywhere, also in countries that no bomb had hit. A month earlier, on 20 November, about 100 million Americans watched the television film 'The Day After', which shows a town in Kansas after a nuclear attack. In the debate that followed, Sagan compared the two superpowers to enemies standing in a room awash in gasoline, one holding nine thousand matches, the other seven thousand.

headline: 1983 in review: the recovery year, shares up 17 percent
text: The S&P 500 gained 17% in 1983 to 164.93; it first closed above 150 on 1 March. The Dow ended at 1,258.64, up 20.3%. Inflation, above 10 percent in 1981, is down to about 3 percent, and unemployment is falling from its peak of 10.8 percent a year ago.

headline: The PC is becoming the office standard
text: IBM's personal computer is selling far beyond the company's own plans, with sales this year put at more than 750,000 machines, and dealers say they receive only part of what they order. Free of the antitrust case, IBM is now present in almost every computer market, and analysts warn that it is becoming dangerous for its competitors.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IBM_Personal_Computer (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_IBM (read 2026-10-03, citing NYT 1983-10-24 and 'Can Anybody Tackle IBM?' 1983-11-26). The 750,000 figure is a full-year count; at the end of December it would have been an estimate.
imageCaption: The IBM PC XT, introduced in 1983
